  Text: [Te179c7b754900e626da5fa0d](#te179c7b754900e626da5fa0d); absolute characters 19114–19214
- **ACT:EO:13694>EO:14110**; S27a52a98d3101e20dd98a07c; {"actor_id":"EO:14110","char_end":31181,"char_start":29642,"confidence":"medium","effective_class":"unknown","effective_date":null,"effective_wording":[{"char_end":4059,"char_start":3864,"text":"Finally, my Administration will help develop effective \nlabeling and content provenance mechanisms, so that Americans are able \nto determine when content is generated using AI and when it is not."},{"char_end":11920,"char_start":11733,"text":"Effective leader-\nship also means pioneering those systems and safeguards needed to deploy \ntechnology responsibly—and building and promoting those safeguards with \nthe rest of the world."},{"char_end":17131,"char_start":16879,"text":"(l) The term ‘‘Federal law enforcement agency’’ has the meaning set forth \nin section 21(a) of Executive Order 14074 of May 25, 2022 (Advancing \nEffective, Accountable Policing and Criminal Justice Practices To Enhance \nPublic Trust and Public Safety)."},{"char_end":27603,"char_start":26208,"text":"(a) Within 90 days of the date of this \norder, to ensure and verify the continuous availability of safe, reliable, \nand effective AI in accordance with the Defense Production Act, as amended, \n50 U.S.C. 4501 et seq., including for the national defense and the protection \nof critical infrastructure, the Secretary of Commerce shall require: \n(i) Companies developing or demonstrating an intent to develop potential \ndual-use foundation models to provide the Federal Government, on an \nongoing basis, with information, reports, or records regarding the following: \n(A) any ongoing or planned activities related to training, developing, \nor producing dual-use foundation models, including the physical and \ncybersecurity protections taken to assure the integrity of that training \nprocess against sophisticated threats; \n(B) the ownership and possession of the model weights of any dual- \nuse foundation models, and the physical and cybersecurity measures taken \nto protect those model weights; and \n(C) the results of any developed dual-use foundation model’s perform-\nance in relevant AI red-team testing based on guidance developed by \nNIST pursuant to subsection 4.1(a)(ii) of this section, and a description \nof any associated measures the company has taken to meet safety objectives, \nsuch as mitigations to improve performance on these red-team tests and \nstrengthen overall model security."},{"char_end":48376,"char_start":47189,"text":"(ii) Within 180 days of the date of this order, the Secretary of Commerce, \nacting through the Director of NIST, in coordination with the Director \nVerDate Sep<11>2014 23:02 Oct 31, 2023 Jkt 262001 PO 00000 Frm 00013 Fmt 4705 Sfmt 4790 E:\\FR\\FM\\01NOE0.SGM 01NOE0ddrumheller on DSK120RN23PROD with PRESDOC-E0\n=== PDF page 12 of 36 ===\n75202 Federal Register / Vol. 88, No. 210 / Wednesday, November 1, 2023 / Presidential Documents \nof OSTP, and in consultation with the Secretary of State, the Secretary \nof HHS, and the heads of other relevant agencies as the Secretary of \nCommerce may deem appropriate, shall initiate an effort to engage with \nindustry and relevant stakeholders, informed by the framework developed \nunder subsection 4.4(b)(i) of this section, to develop and refine for possible \nuse by synthetic nucleic acid sequence providers: \n(A) specifications for effective nucleic acid synthesis procurement screen-\ning; \n(B) best practices, including security and access controls, for managing \nsequence-of-concern databases to support such screening; \n(C) technical implementation guides for effective screening; and \n(D) conformity-assessment best practices and mechanisms."},{"char_end":50295,"char_start":49068,"text":"(iv) In order to facilitate effective implementation of the measures described \nin subsections 4.4(b)(i)–(iii) of this section, the Secretary of Homeland \nSecurity, in consultation with the heads of other relevant agencies as \nthe Secretary of Homeland Security may deem appropriate, shall: \n(A) within 180 days of the establishment of the framework pursuant \nto subsection 4.4(b)(i) of this section, develop a framework to conduct \nstructured evaluation and stress testing of nucleic acid synthesis procure-\nment screening, including the systems developed in accordance with sub-\nsections 4.4(b)(i)–(ii) of this section and implemented by providers of \nsynthetic nucleic acid sequences; and \n(B) following development of the framework pursuant to subsection \n4.4(b)(iv)(A) of this section, submit an annual report to the Assistant \nto the President for National Security Affairs, the Director of the Office \nof Pandemic Preparedness and Response Policy, and the Director of OSTP \non any results of the activities conducted pursuant to subsection \n4.4(b)(iv)(A) of this section, including recommendations, if any, on how \nto strengthen nucleic acid synthesis procurement screening, including cus-\ntomer screening systems. \n4.5."},{"char_end":76011,"char_start":75830,"text":"The report shall include a discussion of issues that may hinder the effective \nuse of AI in research and practices needed to ensure that AI is used respon-\nsibly for research. \n5.3."},{"char_end":112098,"char_start":111612,"text":"The RFI shall seek \nfeedback regarding how privacy impact assessments may be more effective \nat mitigating privacy risks, including those that are further exacerbated \nby AI; and \n(iv) take such steps as are necessary and appropriate, consistent with \napplicable law, to support and advance the near-term actions and long- \nterm strategy identified through the RFI process, including issuing new \nor updated guidance or RFIs or consulting other agencies or the Federal \nPrivacy Council."},{"char_end":115721,"char_start":115253,"text":"(b) To provide guidance on Federal Government use of AI, within 150 \ndays of the date of this order and updated periodically thereafter, the Director \nof OMB, in coordination with the Director of OSTP, and in consultation \nwith the interagency council established in subsection 10.1(a) of this section, \nshall issue guidance to agencies to strengthen the effective and appropriate \nuse of AI, advance AI innovation, and manage risks from AI in the Federal \nGovernment."}],"exceptions_text":[],"filing_date":null,"id":"ACT:EO:13694>EO:14110","names_target":true,"notes":"Machine lead only; no legal ending or revival asserted. Effective wording is ambiguous, section-specific, or has no determinable date.","provision_label":"Sec. 4.","reaches_target_via":"","savings_phrases":[],"scope":"partial","signing_date":"2023-10-30","target_id":"EO:13694","verb":"amend"}

- **ACT:EO:13694>EO:14110@61118f63386c8899**; S8f90c31964dc79feb39d16b5; {"actor_id":"EO:14110","char_end":27672,"char_start":26751,"confidence":"medium","effective_class":"unknown","effective_date":null,"effective_wording":[{"char_end":3277,"char_start":3084,"text":"Finally, my Administration will help develop effective labeling and content provenance mechanisms, so that Americans are able to determine when content is generated using AI and when it is not."},{"char_end":10461,"char_start":10278,"text":"Effective leadership also means pioneering those systems and safeguards needed to deploy technology responsibly—and building and promoting those safeguards with the rest of the world."},{"char_end":15296,"char_start":15049,"text":"(l) The term \"Federal law enforcement agency\" has the meaning set forth in section 21(a) of Executive Order 14074 of May 25, 2022 (Advancing Effective, Accountable Policing and Criminal Justice Practices To Enhance Public Trust and Public Safety)."},{"char_end":23699,"char_start":23363,"text":"(a) Within 90 days of the date of this order, to ensure and verify the continuous availability of safe, reliable, and effective AI in accordance with the Defense Production Act, as amended, 50 U.S.C. 4501 et seq., including for the national defense and the protection of critical infrastructure, the Secretary of Commerce shall require:"},{"char_end":43575,"char_start":43497,"text":"(A) specifications for effective nucleic acid synthesis procurement screening;"},{"char_end":43772,"char_start":43708,"text":"(C) technical implementation guides for effective screening; and"},{"char_end":44798,"char_start":44511,"text":"(iv) In order to facilitate effective implementation of the measures described in subsections 4.4(b)(i)-(iii) of this section, the Secretary of Homeland Security, in consultation with the heads of other relevant agencies as the Secretary of Homeland Security may deem appropriate, shall:"},{"char_end":69411,"char_start":69239,"text":"The report shall include a discussion of issues that may hinder the effective use of AI in research and practices needed to ensure that AI is used responsibly for research."},{"char_end":102185,"char_start":102010,"text":"The RFI shall seek feedback regarding how privacy impact assessments may be more effective at mitigating privacy risks, including those that are further exacerbated by AI; and"},{"char_end":105784,"char_start":105322,"text":"(b) To provide guidance on Federal Government use of AI, within 150 days of the date of this order and updated periodically thereafter, the Director of OMB, in coordination with the Director of OSTP, and in consultation with the interagency council established in subsection 10.1(a) of this section, shall issue guidance to agencies to strengthen the effective and appropriate use of AI, advance AI innovation, and manage risks from AI in the Federal Government."},{"char_end":131513,"char_start":131206,"text":"The function of the White House AI Council is to coordinate the activities of agencies across the Federal Government to ensure the effective formulation, development, communication, industry engagement related to, and timely implementation of AI-related policies, including policies set forth in this order."}],"exceptions_text":[],"filing_date":null,"id":"ACT:EO:13694>EO:14110@61118f63386c8899","names_target":true,"notes":"Machine lead only; no legal ending or revival asserted. Effective wording is ambiguous, section-specific, or has no determinable date.","provision_label":"Sec. 4.","reaches_target_via":"","savings_phrases":[],"scope":"partial","signing_date":"2023-10-30","target_id":"EO:13694","verb":"amend"}

- **ACT:EO:13694>EO:14110@9d656d616c1e7e33**; S730b3b7b83985adcb59a7d82; {"actor_id":"EO:14110","char_end":28229,"char_start":26987,"confidence":"medium","effective_class":"unknown","effective_date":null,"effective_wording":[{"char_end":3400,"char_start":3207,"text":"Finally, my Administration will help develop effective\nlabeling and content provenance mechanisms, so that Americans are able\nto determine when content is generated using AI and when it is not."},{"char_end":10609,"char_start":10424,"text":"Effective leader-\nship also means pioneering those systems and safeguards needed to deploy\ntechnology responsibly—and building and promoting those safeguards with\nthe rest of the world."},{"char_end":15477,"char_start":15228,"text":"(l) The term ‘‘Federal law enforcement agency’’ has the meaning set forth\nin section 21(a) of Executive Order 14074 of May 25, 2022 (Advancing\nEffective, Accountable Policing and Criminal Justice Practices To Enhance\nPublic Trust and Public Safety)."},{"char_end":24975,"char_start":23599,"text":"(a) Within 90 days of the date of this\norder, to ensure and verify the continuous availability of safe, reliable,\nand effective AI in accordance with the Defense Production Act, as amended,\n50 U.S.C. 4501 et seq., including for the national defense and the protection\nof critical infrastructure, the Secretary of Commerce shall require:\n(i) Companies developing or demonstrating an intent to develop potential\ndual-use foundation models to provide the Federal Government, on an\nongoing basis, with information, reports, or records regarding the following:\n(A) any ongoing or planned activities related to training, developing,\nor producing dual-use foundation models, including the physical and\ncybersecurity protections taken to assure the integrity of that training\nprocess against sophisticated threats;\n(B) the ownership and possession of the model weights of any dual-\nuse foundation models, and the physical and cybersecurity measures taken\nto protect those model weights; and\n(C) the results of any developed dual-use foundation model’s perform-\nance in relevant AI red-team testing based on guidance developed by\nNIST pursuant to subsection 4.1(a)(ii) of this section, and a description\nof any associated measures the company has taken to meet safety objectives,\nsuch as mitigations to improve performance on these red-team tests and\nstrengthen overall model security."},{"char_end":44074,"char_start":43183,"text":"(ii) Within 180 days of the date of this order, the Secretary of Commerce,\nacting through the Director of NIST, in coordination with the Director\nof OSTP, and in consultation with the Secretary of State, the Secretary\nof HHS, and the heads of other relevant agencies as the Secretary of\nCommerce may deem appropriate, shall initiate an effort to engage with\nindustry and relevant stakeholders, informed by the framework developed\nunder subsection 4.4(b)(i) of this section, to develop and refine for possible\nuse by synthetic nucleic acid sequence providers:\n(A) specifications for effective nucleic acid synthesis procurement screen-\ning;\n(B) best practices, including security and access controls, for managing\nsequence-of-concern databases to support such screening;\n(C) technical implementation guides for effective screening; and\n(D) conformity-assessment best practices and mechanisms."},{"char_end":45969,"char_start":44757,"text":"(iv) In order to facilitate effective implementation of the measures described\nin subsections 4.4(b)(i)–(iii) of this section, the Secretary of Homeland\nSecurity, in consultation with the heads of other relevant agencies as\nthe Secretary of Homeland Security may deem appropriate, shall:\n(A) within 180 days of the establishment of the framework pursuant\nto subsection 4.4(b)(i) of this section, develop a framework to conduct\nstructured evaluation and stress testing of nucleic acid synthesis procure-\nment screening, including the systems developed in accordance with sub-\nsections 4.4(b)(i)–(ii) of this section and implemented by providers of\nsynthetic nucleic acid sequences; and\n(B) following development of the framework pursuant to subsection\n4.4(b)(iv)(A) of this section, submit an annual report to the Assistant\nto the President for National Security Affairs, the Director of the Office\nof Pandemic Preparedness and Response Policy, and the Director of OSTP\non any results of the activities conducted pursuant to subsection\n4.4(b)(iv)(A) of this section, including recommendations, if any, on how\nto strengthen nucleic acid synthesis procurement screening, including cus-\ntomer screening systems.\n4.5."},{"char_end":69656,"char_start":69477,"text":"The report shall include a discussion of issues that may hinder the effective\nuse of AI in research and practices needed to ensure that AI is used respon-\nsibly for research.\n5.3."},{"char_end":102747,"char_start":102269,"text":"The RFI shall seek\nfeedback regarding how privacy impact assessments may be more effective\nat mitigating privacy risks, including those that are further exacerbated\nby AI; and\n(iv) take such steps as are necessary and appropriate, consistent with\napplicable law, to support and advance the near-term actions and long-\nterm strategy identified through the RFI process, including issuing new\nor updated guidance or RFIs or consulting other agencies or the Federal\nPrivacy Council."},{"char_end":106038,"char_start":105576,"text":"(b) To provide guidance on Federal Government use of AI, within 150\ndays of the date of this order and updated periodically thereafter, the Director\nof OMB, in coordination with the Director of OSTP, and in consultation\nwith the interagency council established in subsection 10.1(a) of this section,\nshall issue guidance to agencies to strengthen the effective and appropriate\nuse of AI, advance AI innovation, and manage risks from AI in the Federal\nGovernment."}],"exceptions_text":[],"filing_date":null,"id":"ACT:EO:13694>EO:14110@9d656d616c1e7e33","names_target":true,"notes":"Machine lead only; no legal ending or revival asserted. Effective wording is ambiguous, section-specific, or has no determinable date.","provision_label":"Sec. 4.","reaches_target_via":"","savings_phrases":[],"scope":"partial","signing_date":"2023-10-30","target_id":"EO:13694","verb":"amend"}

  Text: [Td7eaecad53dfbee1f4b4a4ac](#td7eaecad53dfbee1f4b4a4ac); absolute characters 29642–31181
- **ACT:EO:13694>EO:14117**; Sf9b69c68a0ae5157c023bb73; {"actor_id":"EO:14117","char_end":10384,"char_start":3253,"confidence":"medium","effective_class":"unknown","effective_date":null,"effective_wording":[{"char_end":7344,"char_start":7060,"text":"These risks may be exacerbated when countries of concern use bulk sensitive \npersonal data to develop AI capabilities and algorithms that, in turn, enable \nthe use of large datasets in increasingly sophisticated and effective ways \nto the detriment of United States national security."},{"char_end":12411,"char_start":10434,"text":"(a) To assist in addressing \nthe national emergency described in this order, the Attorney General, in \ncoordination with the Secretary of Homeland Security and in consultation \nwith the heads of relevant agencies, shall issue, subject to public notice \nand comment, regulations that prohibit or otherwise restrict United States \npersons from engaging in any acquisition, holding, use, transfer, transpor-\ntation, or exportation of, or dealing in, any property in which a foreign \ncountry or national thereof has any interest (transaction), where the trans-\naction: \n(i) involves bulk sensitive personal data or United States Government- \nrelated data, as further defined by regulations issued by the Attorney \nGeneral pursuant to this section; \n(ii) is a member of a class of transactions that has been determined \nby the Attorney General, in regulations issued by the Attorney General \npursuant to this section, to pose an unacceptable risk to the national \nsecurity of the United States because the transactions may enable countries \nof concern or covered persons to access bulk sensitive personal data \nor United States Government-related data in a manner that contributes \nto the national emergency described in this order; \n(iii) was initiated, is pending, or will be completed after the effective \ndate of the regulations issued by the Attorney General pursuant to this \nsection; \n(iv) does not qualify for an exemption provided in, or is not authorized \nby a license issued pursuant to, the regulations issued by the Attorney \nGeneral pursuant to this section; and \n(v) is not, as defined by regulations issued by the Attorney General pursuant \nto this section, ordinarily incident to and part of the provision of financial \nservices, including banking, capital markets, and financial insurance serv-\nices, or required for compliance with any Federal statutory or regulatory \nrequirements, including any regulations, guidance, or orders implementing \nthose requirements."}],"exceptions_text":[],"filing_date":null,"id":"ACT:EO:13694>EO:14117","names_target":true,"notes":"Machine lead only; no legal ending or revival asserted. Effective wording is ambiguous, section-specific, or has no determinable date.","provision_label":"","reaches_target_via":"","savings_phrases":[],"scope":"whole","signing_date":"2024-02-28","target_id":"EO:13694","verb":"transfer"}

- **ACT:EO:13694>EO:14117@d5ef386400cc3f15**; S190cdfd375f78f462554a70a; {"actor_id":"EO:14117","char_end":10384,"char_start":3253,"confidence":"medium","effective_class":"unknown","effective_date":null,"effective_wording":[{"char_end":7344,"char_start":7060,"text":"These risks may be exacerbated when countries of concern use bulk sensitive \npersonal data to develop AI capabilities and algorithms that, in turn, enable \nthe use of large datasets in increasingly sophisticated and effective ways \nto the detriment of United States national security."},{"char_end":12411,"char_start":10434,"text":"(a) To assist in addressing \nthe national emergency described in this order, the Attorney General, in \ncoordination with the Secretary of Homeland Security and in consultation \nwith the heads of relevant agencies, shall issue, subject to public notice \nand comment, regulations that prohibit or otherwise restrict United States \npersons from engaging in any acquisition, holding, use, transfer, transpor-\ntation, or exportation of, or dealing in, any property in which a foreign \ncountry or national thereof has any interest (transaction), where the trans-\naction: \n(i) involves bulk sensitive personal data or United States Government- \nrelated data, as further defined by regulations issued by the Attorney \nGeneral pursuant to this section; \n(ii) is a member of a class of transactions that has been determined \nby the Attorney General, in regulations issued by the Attorney General \npursuant to this section, to pose an unacceptable risk to the national \nsecurity of the United States because the transactions may enable countries \nof concern or covered persons to access bulk sensitive personal data \nor United States Government-related data in a manner that contributes \nto the national emergency described in this order; \n(iii) was initiated, is pending, or will be completed after the effective \ndate of the regulations issued by the Attorney General pursuant to this \nsection; \n(iv) does not qualify for an exemption provided in, or is not authorized \nby a license issued pursuant to, the regulations issued by the Attorney \nGeneral pursuant to this section; and \n(v) is not, as defined by regulations issued by the Attorney General pursuant \nto this section, ordinarily incident to and part of the provision of financial \nservices, including banking, capital markets, and financial insurance serv-\nices, or required for compliance with any Federal statutory or regulatory \nrequirements, including any regulations, guidance, or orders implementing \nthose requirements."}],"exceptions_text":[],"filing_date":null,"id":"ACT:EO:13694>EO:14117@d5ef386400cc3f15","names_target":true,"notes":"Machine lead only; no legal ending or revival asserted. wording lead; chronology does not decide legal effect.","provision_text":"Section 1. Policy. It is the policy of the United States to restrict access by countries of concern to Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data when such access would pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States. At the same time, the United States continues to support open, global, interoperable, reliable, and secure flows of data across borders, as well as maintaining vital consumer, economic, scientific, and trade relationships that the United States has with other countries.\n\nThe continuing effort by countries of concern to access Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data threatens the national security and foreign policy of the United States. Such countries' governments may seek to access and use sensitive personal data in a manner that is not in accordance with democratic values, safeguards for privacy, and other human rights and freedoms. Such countries' approach stands in sharp contrast to the practices of democracies with respect to sensitive personal data and principles reflected in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development Declaration on Government Access to Personal Data Held by Private Sector Entities. Unrestricted transfers of Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data to such countries of concern may therefore enable them to exploit such data for a variety of nefarious purposes, including to engage in malicious cyber-enabled activities. Countries of concern can use their access to Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data to track and build profiles on United States individuals, including Federal employees and contractors, for illicit purposes, including blackmail and espionage. Access to Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data by countries of concern through data brokerages, third-party vendor agreements, employment agreements, investment agreements, or other such arrangements poses particular and unacceptable risks to our national security given that these arrangements often can provide countries of concern with direct and unfettered access to Americans' bulk sensitive personal data. Countries of concern can use access to United States persons' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data to collect information on activists, academics, journalists, dissidents, political figures, or members of non-governmental organizations or marginalized communities in order to intimidate such persons; curb dissent or political opposition; otherwise limit freedoms of expression, peaceful assembly, or association; or enable other forms of suppression of civil liberties.\n\nThis risk of access to Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data is not limited to direct access by countries of concern. Entities owned by, and entities or individuals controlled by or subject to the jurisdiction or direction of, a country of concern may enable the government of a country of concern to indirectly access such data. For example, a country of concern may have cyber, national security, or intelligence laws that, without sufficient legal safeguards, obligate such entities and individuals to provide that country's intelligence services access to Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data.\n\nThese risks may be exacerbated when countries of concern use bulk sensitive personal data to develop AI capabilities and algorithms that, in turn, enable the use of large datasets in increasingly sophisticated and effective ways to the detriment of United States national security. Countries of concern can use AI to target United States persons for espionage or blackmail by, for example, recognizing patterns across multiple unrelated datasets to identify potential individuals whose links to the Federal Government would be otherwise obscured in a single dataset.\n\nWhile aspects of this threat have been addressed in previous executive actions, such as Executive Order 13694 of April 1, 2015 (Blocking the Property of Certain Persons Engaging in Significant Malicious Cyber-Enabled Activities), as amended, additional steps need to be taken to address this threat.\n\nAt the same time, the United States is committed to promoting an open, global, interoperable, reliable, and secure Internet; protecting human rights online and offline; supporting a vibrant, global economy by promoting cross-border data flows required to enable international commerce and trade; and facilitating open investment. To ensure that the United States continues to meet these important policy objectives, this order does not authorize the imposition of generalized data localization requirements to store Americans' bulk sensitive personal data or United States Government-related data within the United States or to locate computing facilities used to process Americans' bulk sensitive personal data or United States Government-related data within the United States. This order also does not broadly prohibit United States persons from conducting commercial transactions, including exchanging financial and other data as part of the sale of commercial goods and services, with entities and individuals located in or subject to the control, direction, or jurisdiction of countries of concern, or impose measures aimed at a broader decoupling of the substantial consumer, economic, scientific, and trade relationships that the United States has with other countries. In addition, my Administration has made commitments to increase public access to the results of taxpayer-funded scientific research, the sharing and interoperability of electronic health information, and patient access to their data. The national security restrictions established in this order are specific, carefully calibrated actions to minimize the risks associated with access to bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data by countries of concern while minimizing disruption to commercial activity. This order shall be implemented consistent with these policy objectives, including by tailoring any regulations issued and actions taken pursuant to this order to address the national security threat posed by access to Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data by countries of concern.","sections_touched":["Section 1"],"signing_date":"2024-02-28","source":{"acceptable_as_original":false,"archival_id":"app:node/370086","filing_date":null,"grade":"mirror_transcription","instrument_id":"EO:14117","location_confidence":"medium","location_verified":false,"page_or_item":"Executive Order 14117—Preventing Access to Americans' Bulk Sensitive Personal Data and United States Government-Related Data by Countries of Concern; February 28, 2024; APP node 370086; common-crawl capture 2025-11-11T06:34:11Z","requires_page_check":true,"sha256":"006998d512c2660d9d273ebae3153a2bb45783cfa33dcf72f49872463356fffc","signing_date":"2024-02-28","text_path":"jobs/app-executive-orders/output/texts/executive-order-14117-preventing-access-americans-bulk-sensitive-personal-data-and-united.txt","text_sha256":"5f31428cefaffbe43a0c7eb7d02dd5324da239f14ad870e88d753606a7b5aa52","url":"https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/executive-order-14117-preventing-access-americans-bulk-sensitive-personal-data-and-united"},"verb":"transfer"},{"actor_id":"EO:14117","char_end":9775,"char_start":2644,"confidence":"medium","how_named":"direct","id":"CHAIN:EO:13694#23","notes":"Change wording lead; chronology does not decide legal effect.","provision_text":"Section 1. Policy. It is the policy of the United States to restrict access \nby countries of concern to Americans’ bulk sensitive personal data and \nUnited States Government-related data when such access would pose an \nunacceptable risk to the national security of the United States. At the same \ntime, the United States continues to support open, global, interoperable, \nreliable, and secure flows of data across borders, as well as maintaining \nvital consumer, economic, scientific, and trade relationships that the United \nStates has with other countries. \nThe continuing effort by countries of concern to access Americans’ bulk \nsensitive personal data and United States Government-related data threatens \nthe national security and foreign policy of the United States. Such countries’ \ngovernments may seek to access and use sensitive personal data in a manner \nVerDate Sep<11>2014 22:57 Feb 29, 2024 Jkt 262001 PO 00000 Frm 00003 Fmt 4705 Sfmt 4790 E:\\FR\\FM\\01MRE0.SGM 01MRE0ddrumheller on DSK120RN23PROD with PRESDOC-E0\n=== PDF page 2 of 10 ===\n15422 Federal Register / Vol. 89, No. 42 / Friday, March 1, 2024 / Presidential Documents \nthat is not in accordance with democratic values, safeguards for privacy, \nand other human rights and freedoms. Such countries’ approach stands \nin sharp contrast to the practices of democracies with respect to sensitive \npersonal data and principles reflected in the Organisation for Economic \nCo-operation and Development Declaration on Government Access to Per-\nsonal Data Held by Private Sector Entities. Unrestricted transfers of Ameri-\ncans’ bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related \ndata to such countries of concern may therefore enable them to exploit \nsuch data for a variety of nefarious purposes, including to engage in malicious \ncyber-enabled activities. Countries of concern can use their access to Ameri-\ncans’ bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related \ndata to track and build profiles on United States individuals, including \nFederal employees and contractors, for illicit purposes, including blackmail \nand espionage. Access to Americans’ bulk sensitive personal data and United \nStates Government-related data by countries of concern through data \nbrokerages, third-party vendor agreements, employment agreements, invest-\nment agreements, or other such arrangements poses particular and unaccept-\nable risks to our national security given that these arrangements often can \nprovide countries of concern with direct and unfettered access to Americans’ \nbulk sensitive personal data. Countries of concern can use access to United \nStates persons’ bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government- \nrelated data to collect information on activists, academics, journalists, dis-\nsidents, political figures, or members of non-governmental organizations or \nmarginalized communities in order to intimidate such persons; curb dissent \nor political opposition; otherwise limit freedoms of expression, peaceful \nassembly, or association; or enable other forms of suppression of civil lib-\nerties. \nThis risk of access to Americans’ bulk sensitive personal data and United \nStates Government-related data is not limited to direct access by countries \nof concern. Entities owned by, and entities or individuals controlled by \nor subject to the jurisdiction or direction of, a country of concern may \nenable the government of a country of concern to indirectly access such \ndata. For example, a country of concern may have cyber, national security, \nor intelligence laws that, without sufficient legal safeguards, obligate such \nentities and individuals to provide that country’s intelligence services access \nto Americans’ bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government- \nrelated data. \nThese risks may be exacerbated when countries of concern use bulk sensitive \npersonal data to develop AI capabilities and algorithms that, in turn, enable \nthe use of large datasets in increasingly sophisticated and effective ways \nto the detriment of United States national security. arch_rationale":"Executive Order 13694 (Blocking the Property of Certain Persons Engaging in Significant Malicious Cyber-Enabled Activities; 80 FR 18077) is held in the Federal Register print (FR Doc. 2015-07788) and was read in full. The 22-clause inventory (the opening declaration and sections 1 to 10 with their paragraphs) matches the printed text. Four later orders amend the order: Executive Order 13757 of December 28, 2016, Executive Order 13984 of January 19, 2021, Executive Order 14144 of January 16, 2025 and Executive Order 14306 of June 6, 2025; the 2026 continuation notice names all four. Under the strike-and-insert ruling of 2026-10-21 each amendment is a later event on the clause it changes and the clause continues, amended, until the order ends. The order has no sunset or terminating condition of its own. A sentence-by-sentence search of the first 40 held texts that print the number 13694 (the lookup is capped at 40 files and reports itself truncated) found amendment language in the Executive Order 14306 print and its Federal Register copy, the Executive Order 13848 statement that this order remains in effect, and OFAC notices, and no revocation, supersession, rescission or repeal language aimed at this order. The Federal Register catalog search (later-events:ofr_catalog) returned amendment entries for Executive Orders 13757, 13984, 14144 and 14306 and cross-references between this order and the 2026 notice and Executive Orders 13848, 13849, 14110 and 14117; it returned no revocation or supersession of this order. The other general instrument in the packet, Executive Order 14294 of May 9, 2025 (Fighting Overcriminalization in Federal Regulations), does not print this number and states a prosecution policy for criminal regulatory offenses, which gives no reason to treat any clause as extinguished. Two other leads in the packet do not amend the order: the packet's machine leads from Executive Orders 14304 and 14315 do not print this number in their held texts, and Executive Orders 14110 and 14117 rely on the emergency this order declared but amend nothing in it (Executive Order 14110 was revoked in part by Executive Order 14148 according to the 2026 notice). The Executive Order 13848 print states that Executive Order 13694, as amended by Executive Order 13757, remains in effect. Because the order depends on a declared emergency, the 0 annual continuation notices held for it are attached to every clause; the last, the Notice of March 24, 2026, continues the emergency beyond April 1, 2026, which covers 2026-10-14. Every clause is operative on that date.\nMember checks: {\"earlier_end_check\":\"No earlier end exists for any clause. The order contains no date, duration, condition or performance trigger that could end a clause. The held later instruments are the 0 annual continuation notices, each of which continues the emergency, and no held instrument revokes, supersedes or amends the order. The Notice of March 24, 2026 itself acts under section 202(d) of the National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1622(d)) and the emergency rests on IEEPA, so the principal authorities were still operating in 2026; nothing held shows that any authority cited in the order expired or was repealed.\",\"independent_command_check\":\"The order is a set of continuing commands, prohibitions, findings, definitions, delegations and a reporting authorization. None is a one-time command that was performed and exhausted: entry suspensions apply to an open class and any reporting authorization sets no deadline. No clause is independent of the declared emergency, so one continuing predicate supports all of them. \",\"savings_check\":\"Savings were examined in the held text of the order and in the held later instruments. The order contains no savings or transition provision and no held instrument ends it, so no accrued right or transferred function arises.\",\"scope_check\":\"Each of the 22 clauses was decided separately on the order's own held text, which has no end, read with the 0 held continuation notices and the bounded searches. The packet's current-law leads are sections of the OFAC regulations in 31 CFR (eCFR amended through 2026-11-06) and, where present, U.S. Code sections; their source bytes are not held, so no clause cites them. Definitions, findings and delegations operate only with the blocking command and remain with it. The criteria in section 1(a) have been rewritten in substance twice (by Executive Orders 13757 and 14144) and narrowed to foreign persons by Executive Order 14306; the claim treats each criterion clause as continuing in its amended form and records the before-and-after substance in the clause reasoning. The text of the amended section 1(a) in force on 2026-10-14 is the Executive Order 14144 restatement as edited by Executive Order Order 13694 (Blocking the Property of Certain Persons Engaging in Significant Malicious Cyber-Enabled Activities; 80 FR 18077) is held in the Federal Register print (FR Doc. 2015-07788) and was read in full. The 22-clause inventory (the opening declaration and sections 1 to 10 with their paragraphs) matches the printed text. Four later orders amend the order: Executive Order 13757 of December 28, 2016, Executive Order 13984 of January 19, 2021, Executive Order 14144 of January 16, 2025 and Executive Order 14306 of June 6, 2025; the 2026 continuation notice names all four. Under the strike-and-insert ruling of 2026-10-21 each amendment is a later event on the clause it changes and the clause continues, amended, until the order ends. The order has no sunset or terminating condition of its own. A sentence-by-sentence search of the held texts that print the number 13694 (the Federal Register print, continuation notices, other Federal Register documents and CFR text) for revocation, supersession, rescission, termination, amendment or repeal language next to the number found none. The Federal Register catalog search (later-events:ofr_catalog) returned only cross-references to this order from cyber-related notices and related orders. The other general instrument in the packet, Executive Order 14294 of May 9, 2025 (Fighting Overcriminalization in Federal Regulations), does not print this number and states a prosecution policy for criminal regulatory offenses, which gives no reason to treat any clause as extinguished. Two other leads in the packet do not amend the order: the packet's machine leads from Executive Orders 14304 and 14315 do not print this number in their held texts, and Executive Orders 14110 and 14117 rely on the emergency this order declared but amend nothing in it (Executive Order 14110 was revoked in part by Executive Order 14148 according to the 2026 notice). The Executive Order 13848 print states that Executive Order 13694, as amended by Executive Order 13757, remains in effect. Because the order depends on a declared emergency, the 0 annual continuation notices held for it are attached to every clause; the last, the Notice of March 24, 2026, continues the emergency beyond April 1, 2026, which covers 2026-10-14. Every clause is operative on that date.\nMember checks: {\"earlier_end_check\":\"No earlier end exists for any clause. The order contains no date, duration, condition or performance trigger that could end a clause. The held later instruments are the 0 annual continuation notices, each of which continues the emergency, and no held instrument revokes, supersedes or amends the order. The Notice of March 24, 2026 itself acts under section 202(d) of the National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1622(d)) and the emergency rests on IEEPA, so the principal authorities were still operating in 2026; nothing held shows that any authority cited in the order expired or was repealed.\",\"independent_command_check\":\"The order is a set of continuing commands, prohibitions, findings, definitions, delegations and a reporting authorization. None is a one-time command that was performed and exhausted: entry suspensions apply to an open class and any reporting authorization sets no deadline. No clause is independent of the declared emergency, so one continuing predicate supports all of them. \",\"savings_check\":\"Savings were examined in the held text of the order and in the held later instruments. The order contains no savings or transition provision and no held instrument ends it, so no accrued right or transferred function arises.\",\"scope_check\":\"Each of the 22 clauses was decided separately on the order's own held text, which has no end, read with the 0 held continuation notices and the bounded searches. The packet's current-law leads are sections of the OFAC regulations in 31 CFR (eCFR amended through 2026-11-06) and, where present, U.S. Code sections; their source bytes are not held, so no clause cites them. Definitions, findings and delegations operate only with the blocking command and remain with it. Order 13722 (Blocking Property of the Government of North Korea and the Workers’ Party of Korea, and Prohibiting Certain Transactions With Respect to North Korea; 81 FR 14943) is held in the Federal Register print (FR Doc. 2016-06355) and was read in full. The 36-clause inventory (the opening clause and sections 1 to 13 with their paragraphs) matches the printed text. The order has no sunset or terminating condition of its own. A sentence-by-sentence search of the held texts that print the number 13722 (the Federal Register print, continuation notices, other Federal Register documents and CFR text) for revocation, supersession, rescission, termination, amendment or repeal language next to the number found none. The Federal Register catalog search (later-events:ofr_catalog) returned only cross-references to this order from North Korea notices and related orders. The other general instrument in the packet, Executive Order 14294 of May 9, 2025 (Fighting Overcriminalization in Federal Regulations), does not print this number and states a prosecution policy for criminal regulatory offenses, which gives no reason to treat any clause as extinguished. Executive Order 13722 takes additional steps under the emergency declared in Executive Order 13466, so the held notices continuing that emergency (each from June 2016 on names Executive Order 13722) are the continuation predicate. The later North Korea order held in the packet (Executive Order 13810) recites this order and does not revoke, supersede or amend it. Because the order depends on a declared emergency, the 11 annual continuation notices held for it are attached to every clause; the last, the Notice of June 22, 2026, continues the emergency beyond June 26, 2026, which covers 2026-10-14. Every clause is operative on that date.\nMember checks: {\"earlier_end_check\":\"No earlier end exists for any clause. The order contains no date, duration, condition or performance trigger that could end a clause. The held later instruments are the 11 annual continuation notices, each of which continues the emergency, and no held instrument revokes, supersedes or amends the order. The Notice of June 22, 2026 itself acts under section 202(d) of the National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1622(d)) and the emergency rests on IEEPA, so the principal authorities were still operating in 2026; nothing held shows that any authority cited in the order expired or was repealed.\",\"independent_command_check\":\"The order is a set of continuing commands, prohibitions, findings, definitions, delegations and a reporting authorization. None is a one-time command that was performed and exhausted: entry suspensions apply to an open class and any reporting authorization sets no deadline. No clause is independent of the declared emergency, so one continuing predicate supports all of them. \",\"savings_check\":\"Savings were examined in the held text of the order and in the held later instruments. The order contains no savings or transition provision and no held instrument ends it, so no accrued right or transferred function arises.\",\"scope_check\":\"Each of the 36 clauses was decided separately on the order's own held text, which has no end, read with the 11 held continuation notices and the bounded searches. Order 13722 (Blocking Property of the Government of North Korea and the Workers’ Party of Korea, and Prohibiting Certain Transactions With Respect to North Korea; 81 FR 14943) is held in the Federal Register print (FR Doc. 2016-06355) and was read in full. The 36-clause inventory (the opening clause and sections 1 to 13 with their paragraphs) matches the printed text; the opening clause, which as frozen consists only of the words I hereby order, is widened to include the preamble findings and statement of purpose that precede them. The order has no sunset or terminating condition of its own. A sentence-by-sentence search of the held texts that print the number 13722 (the Federal Register print, continuation notices, other Federal Register documents and CFR text) for revocation, supersession, rescission, termination, amendment or repeal language next to the number found none. The Federal Register catalog search (later-events:ofr_catalog) returned only cross-references to this order from North Korea notices and related orders. The other general instrument in the packet, Executive Order 14294 of May 9, 2025 (Fighting Overcriminalization in Federal Regulations), does not print this number and states a prosecution policy for criminal regulatory offenses, which gives no reason to treat any clause as extinguished. Executive Order 13722 takes additional steps under the emergency declared in Executive Order 13466, so the held notices continuing that emergency (each from June 2016 on names Executive Order 13722) are the continuation predicate. The later North Korea order held in the packet (Executive Order 13810) recites this order and does not revoke, supersede or amend it. Because the order depends on a declared emergency, the 11 annual continuation notices held for it are attached to every clause; the last, the Notice of June 22, 2026, continues the emergency beyond June 26, 2026, which covers 2026-10-14. Every clause is operative on that date.\nMember checks: {\"earlier_end_check\":\"No earlier end exists for any clause. The order contains no date, duration, condition or performance trigger that could end a clause. The held later instruments are the 11 annual continuation notices, each of which continues the emergency, and no held instrument revokes, supersedes or amends the order. The Notice of June 22, 2026 itself acts under section 202(d) of the National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1622(d)) and the emergency rests on IEEPA, so the principal authorities were still operating in 2026; nothing held shows that any authority cited in the order expired or was repealed.\",\"independent_command_check\":\"The order is a set of continuing commands, prohibitions, findings, definitions, delegations and a reporting authorization. None is a one-time command that was performed and exhausted: entry suspensions apply to an open class and any reporting authorization sets no deadline. No clause is independent of the declared emergency, so one continuing predicate supports all of them. \",\"savings_check\":\"Savings were examined in the held text of the order and in the held later instruments. The order contains no savings or transition provision and no held instrument ends it, so no accrued right or transferred function arises.\",\"scope_check\":\"Each of the 36 clauses was decided separately on the order's own held text, which has no end, read with the 11 held continuation notices and the bounded searches. The packet's current-law leads are sections of the OFAC regulations in 31 CFR (eCFR amended through 2026-11-06) and, where present, U.S. Code sections; their source bytes are not held, so no clause cites them. Definitions, findings and delegations operate only with the blocking command and remain with it. ## Valla review leads and component attestations

Preparation attestations never approve legal conclusions or replace whole-case review.
